blocks.text: For calm, clear and harmonious leadership
Conditions for calm & clear leadership
Be calm when dealing with your dog and still consistent and reliable.
Walk calmly and speak in a calm voice.
Stay composed and do not let yourself be provoked.
Your calm becomes your dog's calm.
Keep to pauses and move in a way that is easy for your dog to follow.
Your dog is the way you are. How you present yourself is how your dog presents itself.
Stay relaxed and be harmonious.
Begin every activity with your dog calmly and mentally collected.
Walk in the middle of the path, and over time your dog will walk more calmly.
Do not follow your dog; your dog should learn to walk with you.
Only walk on once calm has settled within you.
Always be present in the moment with your heart, and keep the thinker within you under control.
Communication without words
Use your body language consciously, because it is your dog's mother tongue.
Reduce verbal communication to what is necessary. A glance, a posture or a gesture often says more than words.
Pay attention to your body language. Stay loose, relaxed and inviting.
Tension in your body is transferred directly to your dog.
Learn to read your dog's signals.
Why your calm has a measurable effect on your dog
Dogs perceive the mood of their person very precisely. They react to body tension, breathing, pace and tone of voice.

A Swedish study (Sundman et al., 2019) compared the cortisol levels in the hair of dogs and their owners over several months. The levels of dog and human followed a strikingly similar course. The dog tended to adapt to the stress level of its human rather than the other way round.
Cortisol is a stress hormone. After a strain it is broken down only slowly. Repeated excitement can raise the baseline level over a longer period.
A dog with an elevated stress level is more easily aroused and learns less well. Calm is therefore the prerequisite for any training, not its result.
Your own composure is therefore not a side issue. It is part of the training method.
Recognising stress signals in dogs
Panting without heat or previous exertion.
Licking the nose, yawning and turning the head away.
Hasty sniffing at the ground in situations where there is no reason for it.
Shaking the body as after getting wet, without the dog being wet.
Tense facial expression, retracted corners of the mouth, widened eyes with visible white.
Tail carried low, stiff movements or repeated freezing.
Individual signals are not proof of stress. What matters is the accumulation of signals and the situation in which they occur.
Observation exercise for the next seven days
Observe your dog on walks without intervening and without training.
Note down under “My reflection” at the end of this page in which situations you see stress signals and how you yourself are breathing and moving at that moment.
In these moments, consciously breathe out slowly and observe whether your dog's behaviour changes.
After seven days, compare your notes. Recurring triggers show you where you can start first.

Source: Sundman A.-S. et al. (2019): Long-term stress levels are synchronized in dogs and their owners. Scientific Reports 9, 7391. In the case of persistent stress behaviour, aggression or sudden changes in behaviour, the veterinary practice should first rule out possible pain or illness. If necessary, a behavioural medicine consultation follows.
Patterns to avoid
Avoid restlessness that could unsettle your dog.
Avoid stress; it creates an alarm mood and makes the dog irritable.
Avoid loud and forceful speech. It makes your dog suspect danger or some other challenge.
Avoid haste and hectic activity; they create a mood of departure.
Avoid letting your dog mark permanently at the wayside.
Avoid a lack of rules, so that the dog does not have to take the initiative.
Practice impulse: training calm and composure

On every walk, take 5-10 minutes, later also 30 minutes, in which you do not speak at all and are as free of thoughts as possible. Concentrate only on being in a quiet place with your dog, calmly and in full awareness.
Leadership is not a claim to power, but harmonious, guiding cooperation.
Leadership is inner composure and authority.
If you do not lead, the dog leads.
